name: Claude Certified Architect – Foundations (CCAR-F)
source: Claude Cert Trainer (preguntas originales; explicaciones en español) + preporato/claude-certification-guide y Amey-Thakur/CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS (MIT)
license: Originales: uso personal. Bancos comunitarios: MIT.

questions.stem: In the support agent, a customer requests a €120 refund. What is the correct architecture for enforcing the €50 policy?
options: State the limit in the system prompt and trust the model to escalate.
Enforce the limit in the refund tool/backend (or a pre-tool hook) and route requests above it to a human-approval step.
Give the agent unlimited refunds and audit later.
Ask the customer to confirm twice.
questions.explanation: Políticas de negocio duras → en la herramienta/backend, con escalado humano.

questions.stem: In the research system, one subagent times out and returns nothing. What should the orchestrator do?
options: Silently continue and produce the report with the remaining results.
Retry or reassign the subtask within a bounded budget, and if it still fails, mark the gap explicitly in the final output.
Abort the entire job immediately.
Ask the synthesis step to fill in the missing section from general knowledge.
questions.explanation: Fallo de subagente → reintento acotado y, si no, hueco explícito. Nunca silencio.

questions.stem: Research reports miss sections because the orchestrator splits questions inconsistently. Which change addresses the root cause?
options: Give the orchestrator explicit decomposition guidance and a required output plan (list of sections with owners) before dispatching.
Add more subagents.
Use a larger context window for the synthesizer.
Lower temperature of the subagents.
questions.explanation: Cobertura incompleta → plan explícito de descomposición y comprobación de cobertura.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the orchestrator-workers pattern?
options: A fixed sequence of LLM calls, each processing the previous output.
A central LLM dynamically breaks a task into subtasks, delegates them to workers, and synthesizes results.
Running the same prompt several times and voting.
One LLM generates and another critiques in a loop.
questions.explanation: Orchestrator-workers: descomposición dinámica + delegación + síntesis.

questions.stem: Which TWO signals justify using an autonomous agent rather than a predefined workflow? (Choose TWO.)
options: The number and order of steps cannot be predicted in advance.
Errors are recoverable and the environment provides feedback (e.g., test results) the model can act on.
The task is a fixed three-step transformation.
Strict, low, predictable latency is the top requirement.
questions.explanation: Agente: camino impredecible + feedback del entorno + errores recuperables.

questions.stem: Every action of the support agent must be auditable. What is the best approach?
options: Ask Claude to summarize its actions at the end of each conversation.
Log every tool call (inputs, outputs, user, timestamp, approval) at the tool/hook layer to an append-only store.
Store only the final assistant message.
Enable extended thinking and store the thinking.
questions.explanation: Auditoría = logs deterministas en la capa de herramientas.

questions.stem: Why do subagents help in multi-agent systems?
options: They share one context window, so everything is visible to all.
Each has an isolated context; it can explore deeply and return a condensed result, keeping the orchestrator context clean.
They make every call cheaper.
They remove the need for tool permissions.
questions.explanation: Subagentes = aislamiento de contexto + compresión de resultados.

questions.stem: The team wants shared coding conventions applied for everyone working on a repo, while each engineer keeps personal preferences private. Where should each go?
options: Both in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.
Team conventions in the project CLAUDE.md (committed); personal preferences in the user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (or a local, git-ignored file).
Both in the README.
Team conventions in each engineer's user file.
questions.explanation: Compartido → CLAUDE.md del proyecto en git; personal → usuario/local.

questions.stem: In CI, Claude Code must never push to protected branches. Which control is the most reliable?
options: A line in CLAUDE.md saying "never push to main".
Restrict permissions (deny rules / allowed tools) and use a PreToolUse hook that blocks git push to protected branches, plus branch protection on the repo.
Run Claude Code with --verbose.
Ask reviewers to watch the CI logs.
questions.explanation: Prohibiciones en CI → permisos + hooks + protección del repo.

questions.stem: A PreToolUse hook script wants to block a Bash command and tell Claude why. What should it do?
options: Exit with code 0 and print the reason.
Exit with code 2 and write the reason to stderr (or return a JSON deny decision).
Kill the Claude Code process.
Modify CLAUDE.md at runtime.
questions.explanation: Hook PreToolUse: exit 2 + stderr = bloquear con explicación.

questions.stem: A team repeats the same multi-step "release notes" procedure. They want Claude Code to load the detailed instructions only when relevant. What should they create?
options: Paste the procedure into CLAUDE.md so it is always loaded.
An Agent Skill (SKILL.md with name/description, plus supporting files) loaded on demand.
A new MCP server.
An environment variable.
questions.explanation: Procedimientos reutilizables y bajo demanda → Skills.

questions.stem: An enterprise must guarantee that certain Claude Code settings (e.g., denied tools) cannot be overridden by project or user settings. Where should they be defined?
options: In ~/.claude/settings.json.
In .claude/settings.local.json.
In the managed (enterprise) policy settings, which take precedence.
In CLAUDE.md.
questions.explanation: Lo que no se puede anular → managed settings.

questions.stem: Some claim forms lack the "policy number". Downstream systems reject malformed records, and invented values are unacceptable. How should the extraction schema handle it?
options: Make every field required and instruct Claude to always fill it.
Allow null for genuinely optional fields and instruct Claude to return null when absent, then validate the record.
Default missing fields to "N/A" strings.
Drop the whole form.
questions.explanation: Dato ausente → null permitido, nunca inventado.

questions.stem: Extracted records occasionally fail schema validation. What is a robust recovery pattern?
options: Discard failures silently.
Validate in code; on failure, retry with the validation error fed back to Claude, with a bounded number of attempts, then route to human review.
Retry indefinitely until it passes.
Fix the JSON with regex.
questions.explanation: Validación + reintento con el error + límite + revisión humana.

questions.stem: For extraction from long documents, where should the document be placed relative to the question for best performance?
options: After the question.
Long documents near the top, wrapped in tags, with the instructions/question at the end.
In a separate request.
Placement does not matter.
questions.explanation: Contexto largo arriba, pregunta abajo, todo delimitado con etiquetas.

questions.stem: A classification prompt confuses two similar categories. Which TWO actions are most likely to help? (Choose TWO.)
options: Add contrastive few-shot examples showing borderline cases of both categories.
Define each category precisely, including what it is NOT.
Raise temperature.
Remove the category descriptions to save tokens.
questions.explanation: Categorías confusas → definiciones con límites + ejemplos contrastivos.

questions.stem: The support agent has 35 tools and frequently picks the wrong one. Which change is most effective?
options: Add more tools covering edge cases.
Reduce and consolidate tools, scope each agent/subagent to the tools its task needs, and write precise descriptions with when-to-use guidance.
Rename tools with shorter names.
Switch to temperature 0.
questions.explanation: Selección errónea de herramientas → menos, acotadas y bien descritas.

questions.stem: A tool returns a 2 MB JSON payload, most of which is irrelevant. What is the best design change?
options: Return the full payload; Claude will ignore what it does not need.
Have the tool return only relevant fields (with pagination/filters), plus a concise summary.
Compress the JSON with gzip.
Increase max_tokens.
questions.explanation: Herramientas que devuelven lo justo, con filtros y paginación.

questions.stem: A remote MCP server will be shared by many users over the network. Which transport and auth posture is appropriate?
options: stdio with a shared password in the config file.
Streamable HTTP with proper authorization (OAuth-based per the MCP auth spec) and per-user scopes.
Plain HTTP without auth, behind obscurity.
Embed the server inside the model prompt.
questions.explanation: Servidor MCP remoto multiusuario → HTTP + autorización por usuario.

questions.stem: When is a direct API integration (custom tool in one app) preferable to building an MCP server?
options: When the integration is used by a single application and reuse across clients is not needed.
Always; MCP is deprecated.
When you need the integration in Claude Code, Desktop and your agent.
When you need authorization.
questions.explanation: Uso único → tool directa; reutilización entre clientes → MCP.

questions.stem: A long-running coding agent approaches the context limit after hours of work. Which approach preserves task continuity best?
options: Truncate the oldest messages blindly.
Compact: summarize progress, decisions and open items, clear stale tool outputs, and persist key state in external notes/memory.
Restart the agent from scratch.
Switch to a model with a smaller context.
questions.explanation: Tareas largas → compactación + limpieza de resultados obsoletos + notas externas.

questions.stem: Research reports occasionally cite sources incorrectly. Which reliability measure is most effective?
options: Ask the model to be more careful with citations.
Carry source identifiers with each extracted claim through the pipeline and verify each citation against the source text before publishing.
Remove citations.
Use a higher temperature for diversity.
questions.explanation: Citas fiables → la procedencia viaja con el dato y se verifica.

questions.stem: Which statement about prompt caching in long agent sessions is correct?
options: Caching reduces cost only for the output tokens.
Stable prefixes (system prompt, tool definitions) can be cached so repeated turns cost less and run faster.
Caching guarantees identical outputs.
Caching requires the Batch API.
questions.explanation: Caché de prefijos estables = menos coste y latencia en turnos repetidos.

questions.stem: An extraction pipeline must decide when to send a record to human review. Which signal is most reliable?
options: Claude's self-reported confidence score alone.
Deterministic checks (schema validation, cross-field consistency, missing required fields) combined with calibrated thresholds from labeled data.
Random sampling only.
Response length.
questions.explanation: Escalado a humano → comprobaciones deterministas + umbrales calibrados.

questions.stem: A Claude Code review job in CI produces inconsistent review depth across PRs. What should the team do first?
options: Add a project-level slash command / documented review checklist and run it headlessly with the same instructions every time.
Let each engineer write their own prompt.
Run it interactively.
Disable reviews on large PRs.
questions.explanation: Consistencia en CI → procedimiento versionado (comando/checklist) + headless.

questions.stem: The extraction pipeline must return exactly one JSON object per claim form, conforming to a schema, with no prose. Which configuration is most reliable?
options: Ask for JSON in the system prompt and parse the first `{...}` in the reply.
Define a single extraction tool whose input_schema is the record schema, force it with tool_choice {"type": "tool", "name": "record_claim"}, then validate semantics in code.
Use tool_choice "auto" with ten tools so the model picks the best.
Prefill the assistant turn with "Sure, here is the JSON:".
questions.explanation: Salida fija → herramienta con esquema + tool_choice forzado + validación.

questions.stem: With a forced tool schema in place, records still contain a plausible-looking policy number on forms where none exists. Which TWO changes address this? (Choose TWO.)
options: Make `policy_number` nullable/optional and instruct the model to return null when the form does not contain it.
Add a code check that the extracted value appears verbatim in the source text; route mismatches to review.
Retry the extraction until a policy number is found.
Add stronger wording: "be very careful with policy numbers".
questions.explanation: Datos inventados → esquema que permite null + verificación contra la fuente.

questions.stem: A code-review prompt flags too many low-value issues, and developers ignore it. What is the most effective first change?
options: Tell the model to "only report important issues".
Define explicit reportable categories with severity examples, and temporarily disable the categories that produce most false positives.
Switch to a larger model.
Raise temperature to diversify findings.
questions.explanation: Falsos positivos → criterios explícitos con ejemplos, no "ten cuidado".

questions.stem: A classifier must label support emails as `refund`, `bug`, `account` or `other`. Many emails are ambiguous and get forced into the wrong label. Which design is best?
options: Remove `other` so the model is forced to choose a real category.
Keep `other`, add `unclear` for genuinely ambiguous cases routed to a human, and add 2–4 examples of borderline emails showing the reasoning.
Ask the model for a confidence score and accept anything above 0.9.
Add a paragraph of extra instructions per category.
questions.explanation: Ambigüedad real → valor "unclear" y ejemplos de casos frontera.

questions.stem: The team wants a `/release-notes` command available to everyone who clones the repo, taking the version as an argument. Where and how?
options: In ~/.claude/commands/ on each developer machine.
As a project command/skill file under the repo's .claude/ directory, committed, using an argument placeholder (e.g., $ARGUMENTS) for the version.
As a paragraph in CLAUDE.md describing the steps.
As an MCP server.
questions.explanation: Comando de equipo → fichero de proyecto en .claude/, versionado.

questions.stem: A procedure for database migrations is 400 lines with scripts and templates, used a few times a month. Engineers want Claude Code to apply it only when relevant without bloating every session. What fits best?
options: Put the full procedure in the root CLAUDE.md.
Package it as a Skill (SKILL.md with a precise description, plus the scripts and templates as supporting files).
Create a subagent with the procedure as its system prompt and invoke it for every task.
Paste it into the chat when needed.
questions.explanation: Procedimiento extenso y ocasional → Skill.

questions.stem: Two tools exist: `search_orders(query)` and `find_order(text)`. Claude picks the wrong one about 30% of the time. What should be done first?
options: Add few-shot examples of correct tool choice to the system prompt.
Rewrite both descriptions to state distinct purposes, input formats, examples and when to use each instead of the other—or merge them if they truly overlap.
Add a routing layer with a separate classifier.
Tell the model to "choose carefully".
questions.explanation: Elección errónea de herramienta → descripciones distintas (o fusionar) antes que nada.

questions.stem: The `lookup_customer` tool fails in several ways. Which error response design lets the agent recover best?
options: Return an empty object on any failure.
Return is_error with a category (transient, validation, permission, not_found), whether it is retryable, and a short actionable message.
Return the raw stack trace.
Raise an exception that ends the conversation.
questions.explanation: Errores con categoría y reintentabilidad; nunca vacío.

questions.stem: A custom agent loop stops when the assistant text contains "TASK COMPLETE". Occasionally it stops early or runs forever. What is the correct loop design?
options: Use a more unusual completion phrase.
Continue while stop_reason is "tool_use" (returning every tool_result), stop on "end_turn", and keep a turn/cost budget as a safety limit.
Stop after a fixed 10 iterations.
Ask the model whether it is done after each step.
questions.explanation: El bucle lo controla stop_reason; el tope es solo red de seguridad.

questions.stem: A change touches 14 files across three services and there are two plausible approaches. How should the engineer use Claude Code?
options: Start editing directly and adjust as problems appear.
Use plan mode to explore and compare approaches, agree the plan, then execute; delegate verbose code discovery to an exploration subagent.
Run it headless in CI.
Split into 14 separate sessions, one per file.
questions.explanation: Multifichero o varias alternativas → plan mode primero.

questions.stem: The refund agent needs the order total, the purchase date and the customer's stated reason to decide eligibility. What should the coordinator include when it delegates the task?
questions.context: Customer Support Escalation System: A retailer's support system uses a coordinator agent that receives each customer conversation and delegates to three subagents: an order-lookup agent with read-only order tools, a refund agent that can issue refunds, and a policy agent that searches the returns-policy knowledge base. Company policy: refunds above $250 need a human's approval, and customers can come back to an open conversation within 7 days.
options: The specific facts the refund agent needs, written into the delegation prompt: order id, total, purchase date and the customer's stated reason
Nothing extra, because subagents can read the coordinator's conversation history
The full raw transcript plus every prior tool output, so the refund agent misses nothing
An instruction for the refund agent to ask the customer to repeat the details
questions.explanation: Subagents in a hub-and-spoke design start with their own context window and see only what the coordinator passes to them, so (a) is the working design: the minimum necessary context, stated explicitly. (b) assumes an inheritance that doesn't exist. (c) spends tokens and attention on material the decision doesn't need, which is where lost-in-the-middle errors start. (d) makes the customer pay for a gap the coordinator could close with facts it already has.

questions.stem: Which TWO events should trigger a handoff to a human agent? (Select TWO)
questions.context: Customer Support Escalation System: A retailer's support system uses a coordinator agent that receives each customer conversation and delegates to three subagents: an order-lookup agent with read-only order tools, a refund agent that can issue refunds, and a policy agent that searches the returns-policy knowledge base. Company policy: refunds above $250 need a human's approval, and customers can come back to an open conversation within 7 days.
options: The customer asks to speak to a person
The customer requests a $400 refund for an order the policy covers
The customer writes in capital letters and says they are furious about a covered $90 refund
The model reports a confidence score of 0.62 on its eligibility decision
Answering the customer's question takes three tool calls
questions.explanation: An explicit request for a human ((a)) is a standing escalation trigger, and the $400 refund ((b)) crosses the $250 approval threshold, which makes the handoff mandatory under policy. Sentiment alone ((c)) is no trigger when the request sits inside clear policy; the agent can resolve it while acknowledging the frustration. Self-reported confidence ((d)) is poorly calibrated and makes an unreliable trigger. Task complexity ((e)) is the agent's job.

questions.stem: The policy agent's knowledge-base search sometimes fails because the search service times out, and sometimes finds nothing because no policy covers the case. Both situations currently return an empty list. How should the tool respond instead?
questions.context: Customer Support Escalation System: A retailer's support system uses a coordinator agent that receives each customer conversation and delegates to three subagents: an order-lookup agent with read-only order tools, a refund agent that can issue refunds, and a policy agent that searches the returns-policy knowledge base. Company policy: refunds above $250 need a human's approval, and customers can come back to an open conversation within 7 days.
options: Return a structured error for the timeout (error type, retryable: true, what was attempted) and a successful empty result for the no-match case
Keep returning an empty list in both cases and let the agent retry
Raise an exception in both cases so the coordinator ends the conversation
Return the closest-matching policy in both cases so the agent always has something to cite
questions.explanation: (a) separates a transient failure from a valid empty result, and the two need different recovery: retry the search, or tell the customer no policy applies. With (b), the agent can't tell an outage from a real answer and may report that no policy covers the case during an outage. (c) ends conversations over a recoverable timeout. (d) invents relevance, which leads the agent to cite a policy that doesn't apply.

questions.stem: A customer returns four days later to continue a conversation about a pending refund. Separately, a supervisor wants to test a different resolution on a copy of that conversation without changing what the customer sees. Which pairing fits?
questions.context: Customer Support Escalation System: A retailer's support system uses a coordinator agent that receives each customer conversation and delegates to three subagents: an order-lookup agent with read-only order tools, a refund agent that can issue refunds, and a policy agent that searches the returns-policy knowledge base. Company policy: refunds above $250 need a human's approval, and customers can come back to an open conversation within 7 days.
options: Resume the customer's session so the full history is restored, and fork a separate copy for the supervisor
Fork the session for the customer and resume it for the supervisor
Resume the same session for both
Start fresh sessions for both and paste the last assistant message into each system prompt
questions.explanation: Resuming continues a session with its history intact, which is what the returning customer needs. Forking creates an independent branch from the same history, and changes in the fork never flow back, which is what the supervisor needs. (a) matches both. (b) swaps the two. (c) lets the supervisor's experiment change the customer's conversation. (d) throws away most of the context and relies on one message to carry it.

questions.stem: Which execution pattern fits the scanning stage and the report stage?
questions.context: Multi-Repository Security Audit: A security team runs a nightly audit across 40 repositories. A coordinator spawns one scanner subagent per repository. Each scanner has `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` plus a dependency-check tool. The coordinator merges the findings into one report for the morning stand-up and opens tickets for new critical issues.
options: Fan out the 40 scans in parallel, because they are independent, then run one merge step that builds the report from normalized results
Scan sequentially so each scanner can learn from the previous one's findings, then write the report in parallel sections
Use one agent that scans all 40 repositories in a single context so it can spot cross-repository patterns
Run several report writers in parallel and concatenate their outputs
questions.explanation: Independent work runs in parallel and dependent work runs in sequence, so the hybrid in (a) matches the data dependencies: the scans don't need each other, and the report needs all of them. (b) serializes independent work and slows the audit for no gain. (c) pushes 40 repositories into one context, which degrades attention and turns one failure into a total failure. (d) produces a report with no single view of the findings, which is what the merge step exists for.

questions.stem: Last night the audit crashed at repository 27. The rerun started again from repository 1 and opened duplicate tickets for findings already reported. Which TWO changes fix this? (Select TWO)
questions.context: Multi-Repository Security Audit: A security team runs a nightly audit across 40 repositories. A coordinator spawns one scanner subagent per repository. Each scanner has `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` plus a dependency-check tool. The coordinator merges the findings into one report for the morning stand-up and opens tickets for new critical issues.
options: Checkpoint progress to a manifest file (completed repositories, pending repositories, results so far) and resume from it after a crash
Make ticket creation idempotent, for example keyed by repository and finding id, so a replay can't create duplicates
Give the scanners larger context windows so they remember the previous run
Ask the coordinator at startup which repositories it already finished
Run the audit weekly instead of nightly
questions.explanation: A manifest ((a)) lets the restarted coordinator continue from repository 27, and idempotent side effects ((b)) make any replayed step harmless; together they turn a crash into a delay. Context windows ((c)) don't survive a process crash, and the coordinator has no memory of the previous run to ask about ((d)), because the API is stateless. Running less often ((e)) leaves the failure in place.

questions.stem: An engineer proposes giving every scanner the full tool set, including `Write`, `Bash` and the ticketing tool, 'in case they need it.' What is the best response?
questions.context: Multi-Repository Security Audit: A security team runs a nightly audit across 40 repositories. A coordinator spawns one scanner subagent per repository. Each scanner has `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` plus a dependency-check tool. The coordinator merges the findings into one report for the morning stand-up and opens tickets for new critical issues.
options: Keep each scanner on the read-only tools its job needs, and let only the coordinator open tickets from the merged findings
Accept the proposal, because more tools make the scanners more capable
Give the scanners every tool and add a system-prompt rule forbidding writes
Replace the scanner tools with Bash alone, since Bash can do everything the other tools do
questions.explanation: Least privilege scopes each agent to what its responsibility requires. (a) also keeps tool selection accurate and stops a misbehaving scanner from changing code or opening tickets. (b) widens the blast radius and adds selection noise for capabilities nobody uses. (c) relies on a probabilistic instruction to restrain a capability that should never be there. (d) hands the scanners the broadest tool of all.

questions.stem: The morning report said 'No critical issues found across all repositories.' The team later learns that six scanners hit their token budgets and skipped their largest files. What should the report format have required?
questions.context: Multi-Repository Security Audit: A security team runs a nightly audit across 40 repositories. A coordinator spawns one scanner subagent per repository. Each scanner has `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` plus a dependency-check tool. The coordinator merges the findings into one report for the morning stand-up and opens tickets for new critical issues.
options: A coverage annotation from every scanner (files reviewed, files skipped with reasons, coverage counts) carried into the merged report
A confidence score from each scanner
A longer narrative summary from each scanner
Nothing; the scanners needed a more capable model
questions.explanation: Without explicit coverage, 'no issues found' can't be told apart from 'no issues found in the part that ran.' (a) makes the gap visible so the skipped files can be queued for a focused pass. Self-reported confidence ((b)) is poorly calibrated and says nothing about what was skipped. A longer summary ((c)) adds words without the counts. A stronger model ((d)) can still hit a budget, and the report would still hide it.

questions.stem:
After the first tool call, every follow-up request in your agent loop fails with a 400 error. Here is how the loop builds the next request. What is wrong?

```python
response = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024,
                                  tools=tools, messages=messages)
if response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    call = next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use")
    result = run_tool(call.name, call.input)
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [{
        "type": "tool_result",
        "tool_use_id": call.id,
        "content": result,
    }]})
```
options: The assistant turn containing the `tool_use` block is never appended, so the `tool_result` refers to a call the next request doesn't contain
`tool_result` blocks belong in the system prompt
`max_tokens` is too low for a tool loop
The loop should set `tool_choice` to `any` after the first call
questions.explanation: The API is stateless, so each request must carry the whole exchange: the assistant message with the `tool_use` block comes first, then the user message with the matching `tool_result` ((a)). Without it, the `tool_use_id` points at nothing. (b) misplaces tool results, which go in a user turn. (c) and (d) change settings that have nothing to do with a malformed history.

questions.stem: Your research agent uses the server-side web search tool. Some responses come back with `stop_reason` `pause_turn`, and the loop treats them as finished, returning half-done research. What is the correct handling?
options: Send a follow-up request with the paused assistant response appended as-is, so Claude can continue the server-side work
Treat `pause_turn` the same as `end_turn`
Run the web search locally and return a `tool_result` for it
Raise `max_tokens` and send the original request again
questions.explanation: `pause_turn` means a server-side tool loop reached its iteration limit mid-task. The documented handling is (a): return the response as the latest assistant turn, and Claude picks up where it stopped. (b) is the bug in the question. (c) treats a server tool like a client tool; there is no `tool_use` for your code to answer. (d) restarts the work and pays for it twice.

questions.stem: A team answers one-line FAQ questions from a two-page policy with a six-subagent pipeline: retriever, reader, drafter, tone checker, fact checker and formatter. Answers take 25 seconds and cost far more than expected. What is the best change?
options: Collapse it to a single model call with the policy in context, plus a lightweight validation step if needed
Run the six subagents in parallel under a coordinator
Move every subagent to the most capable model to cut retries
Cache each subagent's output
questions.explanation: This is over-decomposition: the task is small, single-domain and fits in one context, so the subagents add orchestration cost without any isolation benefit, and (a) removes the overhead. Parallelizing ((b)) doesn't fit a chain where each step needs the previous step's output. (c) raises the cost of a design that shouldn't exist. (d) helps only with repeated identical questions and leaves the latency of the chain in place.

questions.stem: A payments service's error rate spiked. The cause could be in code, configuration, infrastructure or a third-party API, and what to check next depends on what each check finds. How should the coordinator decompose the investigation?
options: Dynamic decomposition: plan the next subtasks from each finding, with a token budget and iteration cap enforced in code as safety nets
A fixed pipeline that runs the four checks in a set order
Run every conceivable check in parallel with no coordinator
One prompt asking Claude for the root cause
questions.explanation: Open-ended investigations, where the next step depends on what you just learned, call for dynamic decomposition. Because that pattern costs more and can wander, (a) pairs it with limits enforced outside the model. A fixed pipeline ((b)) suits workflows that are known in advance. (c) wastes effort and leaves nobody to connect the findings. (d) asks for an answer without giving the model any way to gather evidence.

questions.stem: Long research tasks sometimes use ten times the expected tokens. Which TWO belong in a reliable token-budget design? (Select TWO)
options: Track cumulative input and output tokens from each response's usage field inside the loop
Stop the loop in code when the budget is reached, with a wrap-up instruction injected at about 80% of the budget
A system-prompt instruction asking Claude to stay under 50,000 tokens
Asking Claude each turn how many tokens it has used so far
Setting `max_tokens` to 50 on every call
questions.explanation: Budgets are enforced from outside the model: measure from the usage field ((a)) and act on the measurement with a soft warning and a hard stop ((b)). An instruction ((c)) and the model's own estimate ((d)) are probabilistic and unmeasured. A tiny `max_tokens` ((e)) truncates every response, so turns end at the cap before they finish.

questions.stem: A team's MCP server should (1) let Claude create Jira tickets, (2) expose the team's API schema files so a user can attach them as context, and (3) provide a reusable 'triage this incident' template with the team's severity rubric. Which MCP primitives fit, in that order?
options: Tool, resource, prompt
Tool, tool, tool
Resource, tool, prompt
Prompt, resource, tool
questions.explanation: Creating a ticket is an action, so it's a tool. Schema files are read-only data for the client to browse and attach, so they're a resource. The packaged triage template is a prompt. (a) matches action, data and know-how in that order. (b) turns data and a template into callable functions. (c) and (d) put the action in the wrong primitive.

questions.stem: Every developer on a team should get the same internal MCP server in Claude Code, and the server needs an API token. Which TWO choices are correct? (Select TWO)
options: Define the server in the project's `.mcp.json` and commit it to the repository
Reference the token in `.mcp.json` as `${INTERNAL_API_TOKEN}` and have each developer set that environment variable
Paste the raw token into `.mcp.json` so setup is a single step
Have each developer add the server with local scope by following a wiki page
Put the token in `CLAUDE.md` so Claude can pass it to the server
questions.explanation: Project scope ((a)) is the configuration that reaches the whole team through version control, and environment variable expansion ((b)) keeps the secret out of the repository. (c) commits a credential. (d) relies on every developer repeating a manual step, and local scope never propagates. (e) puts a secret into the model's context, where it can leak through outputs or logs.

questions.stem: When users ask to change their email address, Claude often calls `get_customer` instead of `update_customer`, then tells the user the change is done. Both tools exist. What is the first fix?
options: Rewrite both descriptions: what each tool does, when to use it, and when to use the other one instead, with `get_customer` described as read-only
Rename `get_customer` to `fetch_customer`
Add a system-prompt line telling Claude to use `update_customer` for updates
Remove `get_customer` from the agent
questions.explanation: Claude selects tools mainly from their descriptions, so overlapping or vague descriptions are the first thing to fix ((a)), and the boundary statements ('to change a record, use `update_customer`') are what resolve this confusion. A rename ((b)) changes little while the descriptions stay vague. A system-prompt patch ((c)) is weaker than fixing the routing signal itself. Removing the read tool ((d)) breaks every legitimate lookup.

questions.stem: Your team wants every file Claude edits to be formatted with Prettier immediately after each edit, for everyone working in the repository. Which configuration does that?
options: A `PostToolUse` hook in the committed `.claude/settings.json`, matching `Edit|Write`, that runs Prettier on the edited file
A `PreToolUse` hook on `Edit` that runs Prettier
A `CLAUDE.md` line: 'Run Prettier after every edit'
A hook in each developer's `~/.claude/settings.json`
questions.explanation: Formatting has to run after the file changes, which is `PostToolUse`, and the committed project settings file shares the hook with the whole team, so (a) covers both requirements. (b) runs before the edit exists. (c) is guidance Claude may skip, while a hook runs every time. (d) works only for developers who set it up themselves.

questions.stem: A team requires that Claude never ends its work while the test suite is failing. Which hook enforces this?
options: A `Stop` hook that runs the tests and exits with code 2, printing the failures to stderr, when any test fails
A `SessionEnd` hook that runs the tests
A `UserPromptSubmit` hook that runs the tests before each prompt
A `PostToolUse` hook that runs the tests after every file read
questions.explanation: Exit code 2 from a `Stop` hook prevents Claude from stopping and feeds the stderr text back, so Claude keeps working on the failures ((a)). `SessionEnd` ((b)) fires as the session closes and can't block anything. (c) tests before the work happens. (d) runs constantly at the wrong moment and can't stop Claude from finishing.

questions.stem: A `PostToolUse` hook on `Write` scans each file Claude writes. It finds an API key in a file Claude just wrote and exits with code 2. What happens?
options: The file has already been written; Claude receives the hook's stderr message and can act on it, for example by removing the key
The write is cancelled and the file is never created
Claude Code shuts down the session
Nothing happens, because exit code 2 is ignored for `PostToolUse`
questions.explanation: `PostToolUse` fires after the tool has run, so it can't undo the write; exit code 2 shows its stderr to Claude ((a)). To stop the write itself, the check belongs in a `PreToolUse` hook, where exit code 2 blocks the call, which is the behavior (b) describes. (c) and (d) describe behaviors that don't exist.

questions.stem: A developer asks Claude Code to migrate 40 files from a callback-based API client to async/await. The change touches shared types, and there are two reasonable migration strategies. What is the best way to start?
options: Plan Mode: let Claude explore the codebase and propose a migration plan to review before any file changes
Direct execution, file by file, fixing problems as they appear
One prompt for the whole change, then review the final diff
A `CLAUDE.md` rule saying 'use async/await'
questions.explanation: Multi-file, cross-cutting changes with more than one valid approach are Plan Mode's case ((a)): the strategy gets agreed before 40 files move. (b) and (c) commit to an approach before anyone has compared the options, and a wrong choice is expensive to unwind. (d) states a preference without planning the migration.

questions.stem: A team's dependency-audit skill prints thousands of lines of output, and teammates complain it floods the main conversation. Which frontmatter change fixes this?
options: `context: fork`, so the skill runs in an isolated subagent and returns its result
`disable-model-invocation: true`
`allowed-tools: Read`
`model: haiku`
questions.explanation: `context: fork` ((a)) runs the skill in its own subagent context, so the verbose work stays out of the main conversation. (b) only stops Claude from invoking the skill automatically; the output still floods the conversation whenever someone runs it. (c) changes which tools are pre-approved and (d) changes the model, and neither moves the output.

questions.stem: In a monorepo, files under `services/payments/` follow strict rules (all amounts in integer cents, no floats). The rules confuse Claude when it works on the frontend. Which TWO placements load these rules only when Claude works in the payments code? (Select TWO)
options: A file in `.claude/rules/` with `paths: ["services/payments/**"]` in its frontmatter
A `CLAUDE.md` file inside `services/payments/`
A section titled 'Payments only' in the root `CLAUDE.md`
Each developer's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`
The project's `.mcp.json`
questions.explanation: A path-scoped rule ((a)) loads when Claude reads or edits a matching file, and a subdirectory `CLAUDE.md` ((b)) loads on demand when Claude works with files in that directory. The root `CLAUDE.md` ((c)) loads in every session, frontend work included. (d) is personal and reaches nobody else. (e) configures MCP servers and holds no instructions.

questions.stem: A code-review prompt says 'Be thorough but avoid nitpicks.' Reviews flag style issues inconsistently and miss SQL injection. Which rewrite fixes the cause?
options: 'Report only these issues: SQL injection, XSS, authentication bypass and secrets in code. Report high or critical severity only. Do not comment on formatting or naming.'
'Be extremely thorough and never miss anything.'
'Be conservative with your comments.'
'You are a world-class senior security engineer.'
questions.explanation: Vague instructions produce inconsistent behavior because the model has to guess the threshold. (a) names the categories, the severity floor and the exclusions, and anyone reading a review can check whether it followed them. (b) and (c) push the same vague guidance in two directions. A role line ((d)) without criteria leaves the same guesswork.

questions.stem: A classifier should flag support tickets that mention a physical safety risk. In testing it flags every ticket containing the word 'fire', including 'firewall rules reset after update.' What is the best few-shot improvement?
options: Two to four examples that include the firewall ticket labeled not-safety with a one-line reason, a genuine safety ticket, and an ambiguous case
Twenty examples of genuine safety tickets
An instruction: 'Don't be fooled by keywords.'
A lower temperature
questions.explanation: Few-shot examples teach reasoning and edge cases best when they include something the model should leave alone, so the tricky negative in (a) is the example that matters. (b) piles on positives and teaches nothing about the false positives. (c) is vague guidance. Temperature ((d)) changes randomness and leaves the misunderstanding in place.

questions.stem: Your team plans to use structured outputs (a JSON schema in `output_config.format`) for invoice extraction. Which TWO statements about this feature are true? (Select TWO)
options: Constrained decoding makes the response valid JSON that matches the schema's structure and types
A refusal or a `max_tokens` cutoff can still produce output that doesn't match the schema, so check `stop_reason`
It guarantees the extracted values are correct for the source document
It removes the need to validate business rules, such as totals matching line items
It works only when `tool_choice` forces a specific tool
questions.explanation: Structured outputs guarantee format: valid, schema-compliant JSON ((a)), with the documented exceptions of refusals and truncation ((b)). Format says nothing about whether the values are right, so semantic checks such as totals and dates stay in your pipeline, which rules out (c) and (d). (e) confuses the feature with forced tool use; structured outputs are requested through `output_config.format`.

questions.stem: An extraction fails validation because `invoice_date` came back as 2026-04-31, a date that doesn't exist. What should the retry request contain?
options: The original document, the failed output, and the specific error ('`invoice_date` 2026-04-31 is not a valid date'), with an instruction to correct only that field
The original document again with no other changes
The failed output and the words 'try again'
The same request sent to a more capable model
questions.explanation: A useful retry tells the model exactly what failed and gives it the source to fix it against ((a)). (b) repeats the conditions that produced the error. (c) removes the source the model needs to correct the date. (d) changes the model without telling it what went wrong.

questions.stem: A product team wants to move its live chat assistant to the Message Batches API to cut costs in half. What is the right assessment?
options: Reject it: batches carry no latency guarantee (most finish within an hour, some take up to 24), so a waiting user can't be served; cut costs with prompt caching or by routing routine messages to a cheaper tier
Approve it: the same quality at half the price
Approve it, provided the app polls for results every second
Reject it, because batch requests can't include a system prompt
questions.explanation: The batch discount comes with asynchronous processing and no latency guarantee, which rules it out for anyone waiting on an answer ((a)). (b) ignores the latency. Polling ((c)) doesn't speed up processing. (d) is false: batch requests take the same parameters as regular Messages requests.

questions.stem: One prompt asks Claude to extract 30 fields from a contract, normalize every currency, classify the risk clauses and write an executive summary. Results vary from run to run, and errors are hard to trace. What is the best restructuring?
options: A chain of focused prompts (extract, validate, normalize, classify, summarize), each with its own instructions and checks
The same single prompt with each requirement marked IMPORTANT
The same single prompt on a more capable model
Ask for the executive summary first, then the fields
questions.explanation: Prompt chaining gives each stage one job and a validation point, so a failure shows up in the stage that caused it ((a)). Emphasis ((b)) doesn't reduce the number of jobs in one prompt. A stronger model ((c)) may help a little and leaves errors untraceable. Reordering ((d)) builds the summary on fields nobody has checked yet.

questions.stem: A knowledge-base Q&A agent receives 40 retrieved passages per question. The passage with the answer usually lands near the middle, and answers often miss it. Which TWO changes address this? (Select TWO)
options: Re-rank the passages and pass only the most relevant few
Put the passages first and the question and instructions at the end of the prompt
Switch to a model with a larger context window
Retrieve 80 passages instead of 40
Raise the temperature
questions.explanation: Attention is weakest in the middle of long contexts, so the fixes shrink the middle and move what matters to the edges: fewer, better passages ((a)), and long material first with the question last, which Anthropic's long-context guidance recommends ((b)). A bigger window ((c)) and more passages ((d)) make the middle longer. Temperature ((e)) affects randomness and does nothing for attention.

questions.stem: Two internal documents disagree about the warranty period: a 2024 policy says 12 months and a 2026 update says 24 months. What should the agent's answer do?
options: Give the answer with attribution: both values, their documents and dates, the newer one identified as likely current, and the conflict flagged for review
State 24 months without mentioning the conflict, because the newer document wins
Average the two and state 18 months
Decline to answer until someone fixes the documents
questions.explanation: Provenance keeps each claim tied to its source and surfaces conflicts instead of settling them silently ((a)). Silently picking one value ((b)) is the tested anti-pattern even when the choice happens to be right, because nobody learns that the documents disagree. (c) produces a number neither source supports. (d) withholds an answer the agent can give with a caveat.

questions.stem: Your support agent resolves most tickets but sometimes loops indefinitely, re-calling lookup_order on the same order. What is the correct structural fix?
options: Raise max_tokens so the loop has room to finish
Remove the lookup_order tool
Add explicit loop-termination conditions: cap tool iterations, detect repeated identical calls, and route to escalate_to_human when progress stalls
Lower the temperature
questions.explanation: Agent loops need engineered termination: iteration budgets, repeated-call detection, and an escalation path when the agent cannot progress. Token budget (A) delays the symptom, removing a needed tool (B) breaks resolution, and temperature (D) does not bound iteration.

questions.stem: process_refund currently accepts any amount. Support policy caps agent-initiated refunds at $200; larger refunds need a human. Where does that rule belong?
options: In the system prompt, phrased firmly
In the model's reasoning, since it reads the policy
In quarterly staff training
Enforced in the tool layer: the tool rejects amounts over the cap with a structured error, and a hook or the tool itself routes larger cases to escalation
questions.explanation: Hard policy limits are enforced deterministically at the tool boundary, not requested of the model. Prompt phrasing (A) and model reasoning (B) are probabilistic where the requirement is absolute, and training (C) does not constrain the agent at all.

questions.stem: Your coordinator delegates to search, analysis, and report subagents. Final reports cite sources that do not support their claims, though each subagent behaves sensibly alone. What is the most likely architectural cause?
options: Provenance is lost at handoffs: findings and their sources are not passed together in a structured form, so the report writer pairs claims with citations by guesswork
The report subagent's model is too small
The web is unreliable
Too many subagents are running in parallel
questions.explanation: In multi-agent pipelines, provenance survives only if the handoff format carries claim and source together. That failure mode produces exactly this symptom while every stage looks locally fine. Model size (B), source quality (C), and parallelism (D) do not explain correct facts paired with wrong citations.

questions.stem: The analysis subagent returns 30,000-token document dumps to the coordinator, which then fails on context limits. What is the right fix?
options: Give the coordinator a bigger context window
Have subagents return structured extracts, findings with citations and confidence, while full documents stay in the subagent's context or a scratchpad file
Have the coordinator drop the oldest messages silently
Run the analysis twice and keep the shorter answer
questions.explanation: Context isolation is the point of subagent delegation: raw bulk stays at the edge, distilled results travel. A larger window (A) postpones the failure, silent dropping (C) loses arbitrary information, and rerunning (D) changes nothing structural.

questions.stem: Your monorepo has frontend and backend directories with different conventions, and one team-wide rule about commit style. Where does each piece of configuration belong?
options: Everything in one root CLAUDE.md
Each engineer's personal user-level CLAUDE.md
The commit rule in the project-level CLAUDE.md; the per-area conventions in path-scoped rules under .claude/rules/ that load only when matching files are touched
A wiki page linked from the README
questions.explanation: The hierarchy exists for exactly this: shared rules at project scope, conditional conventions path-scoped so context is spent only where relevant. One root file (A) loads everything everywhere, personal files (B) diverge per engineer, and a wiki (D) never reaches the model.

questions.stem: Your CI job runs Claude Code to review pull requests, and the pipeline must parse the results mechanically. Which invocation is correct?
options: Interactive mode with a human copying the output into CI
Plan mode, which is safer for automation
A shell script that greps the human-readable transcript
Non-interactive mode with -p, with --output-format json and a schema so the review arrives as machine-readable, validated output
questions.explanation: Headless CI use is what -p with JSON output and a schema is for: deterministic invocation, parseable results. A human in the loop (A) is not CI, plan mode (B) is a review gate for interactive work rather than an output format, and grepping prose (C) breaks on the first wording change.

questions.stem: The automated reviewer flags dozens of trivial style nits per pull request, and engineers have started ignoring it. Which change addresses the false-positive problem the way the blueprint suggests?
options: Define explicit review criteria in the prompt: what to flag, what to ignore, and a severity bar, with a few worked examples of in-scope and out-of-scope findings
Run the review twice and post only findings that appear both times
Cap the reviewer at three findings per pull request
Route all findings to a channel nobody reads
questions.explanation: Precision comes from explicit criteria and few-shot examples that draw the boundary between signal and noise. Double-running (B) filters randomness but not systematic nit-picking, an arbitrary cap (C) drops real findings on bad days, and (D) is surrender.

questions.stem: Invoices sometimes lack a purchase-order number, and your extraction schema must handle that honestly while catching real misses. What is the right schema design?
options: Make every field required so nothing is missed
Make purchase_order nullable, so absence is recorded as null, and validate that it is present whenever the document type requires it
Make everything optional to avoid validation errors
Have the model invent a plausible number when one is missing
questions.explanation: Schema design encodes reality: genuinely optional data is nullable, and conditional requirements are validated downstream. All-required (A) forces fabrication or failure on legitimate documents, all-optional (C) blinds you to true misses, and invention (D) is data corruption.

questions.stem: Your pipeline reports 98% field accuracy, measured on the documents the schema validated cleanly. An auditor calls the number misleading. Why?
options: Accuracy should be measured only on the hardest documents
98% is below industry standard
Validation-clean documents are a biased sample: the honest measure comes from a labeled sample drawn across all documents, including ones that failed or barely passed validation
Field accuracy is not a real metric
questions.explanation: Measuring only where the system already succeeded inflates the estimate; calibration requires a labeled sample representative of the full input stream. Hardest-only (A) biases in the opposite direction, the standard claim (B) is invented, and (D) is false.

questions.stem: Your codebase-exploration agent has get_file_contents, read_source, and fetch_file tools that all read files, and it frequently picks poorly among them. What is the correct fix?
options: Add a fourth, better file-reading tool
Fine-tune the model on the tool list
Randomize which tool the harness dispatches
Consolidate to one file-reading tool, or give the survivors sharply differentiated descriptions that state exactly when each applies
questions.explanation: Tool selection runs on descriptions; overlapping tools with vague descriptions produce dithering. Consolidation or sharp differentiation is the documented cure. Adding overlap (A) worsens it, fine-tuning (B) is disproportionate, and randomization (C) institutionalizes the confusion.

questions.stem: A support workflow resolves tickets by looking up an account, checking entitlement, and drafting a reply, always in that order. Which architecture is correct?
options: A deterministic pipeline that calls the model at each defined step
A single agent that decides each step at runtime
Three agents that negotiate the order between them
One prompt containing all three steps
questions.explanation: A known, fixed sequence should be encoded rather than rediscovered on every run, which makes it cheaper, faster, and testable step by step. Runtime decisions (B, C) add nondeterminism for no gain, and one prompt (D) removes the checkpoints between steps.

questions.stem: What is the strongest justification for splitting work across subagents?
options: The task has many steps
Separate lines of work each need their own context, and mixing them degrades both
Subagents are faster than a single agent
The output must be assembled from several sections
questions.explanation: Subagents exist to isolate context, so the case for them is contamination between concerns rather than volume. Step count (A) and sectioned output (D) suit a workflow, and delegation usually adds latency rather than removing it (C).

questions.stem: An agent loops between two tools without converging. What is the most appropriate first control?
options: Increase the context window so it can see more history
Switch to a larger model
Impose a step ceiling and define the terminating condition explicitly
Remove one of the two tools
questions.explanation: Non-termination is bounded by an explicit stop condition and a hard ceiling, which contains cost and makes the failure visible. More context (A) and a larger model (B) do not guarantee convergence, and removing a tool (D) may break the task.

questions.stem: Which property most increases the operational risk of an agentic design?
options: It calls more than one model
It produces structured output
It runs longer than a minute
It takes irreversible actions without a checkpoint
questions.explanation: Reversibility governs the cost of being wrong, which is the dominant risk in autonomous execution. Multiple models (A), structure (B), and duration (C) affect cost and complexity rather than blast radius.

questions.stem: How should an agentic system handle a step whose result it cannot verify?
options: Surface the unverifiable step for human confirmation before acting on it
Proceed, since the model is usually right
Retry the step until two runs agree
Log the step and continue
questions.explanation: An unverifiable result is exactly where human judgment belongs, before it is acted upon. Assuming correctness (B) and logging without stopping (D) both act on unchecked output, and agreement across runs (C) establishes consistency rather than truth.

questions.stem: A team proposes an agent for a task where every input is well formed and every rule is known. What should the architect recommend?
options: An agent, for future flexibility
A deterministic implementation, reserving model calls for the genuinely ambiguous parts
An agent with a low step limit
A multi-agent design for separation of concerns
questions.explanation: Known rules over well-formed input are code, and using a model there buys nondeterminism at a price. Speculative flexibility (A), a constrained agent (C), and multiple agents (D) all keep the cost without the need.

questions.stem: What most improves the debuggability of an agentic system in production?
options: Reducing the number of tools
Using a single model for every step
Recording the inputs, tool calls, and outputs of each step as a trace
Increasing the step limit
questions.explanation: A per-step trace is what makes a nondeterministic run reconstructable after the fact. Fewer tools (A) and one model (B) simplify without explaining, and a higher ceiling (D) makes failures longer rather than clearer.

questions.stem: Where should conventions that apply to everyone working in a repository be recorded?
options: In each developer's personal settings
In the pull request template
In a pinned chat message
In a CLAUDE.md committed to the repository
questions.explanation: Committed project memory is versioned, reviewable, and shared, which is what a team convention requires. Personal settings (A) do not propagate, and templates (B) and messages (C) are not read as working context.

questions.stem: What distinguishes work suited to headless mode?
options: It is well defined and repeatable, so it can run unattended in automation
It is complex and needs close supervision
It requires many tools
It produces a long output
questions.explanation: Headless execution suits bounded, repeatable work where no one is watching. Supervision (B) argues for interactive use, and tool count (C) and output length (D) do not determine suitability.

questions.stem: A skill and a subagent could both address a need. What decides between them?
options: Skills are always preferable
Whether the need is reusable know-how or an isolated line of work with its own context
Whether the task is long
Whether the repository already has a CLAUDE.md
questions.explanation: The two solve different problems: a skill packages reusable procedure, a subagent isolates context. A blanket preference (A), duration (C), and existing files (D) do not address that distinction.

questions.stem: What is the correct use of a hook in a Claude Code workflow?
options: To hold instructions the model should follow
To store project context
To enforce a deterministic action at a defined point, independently of the model
To define which model is used
questions.explanation: Hooks run as code at fixed points, so they enforce rather than request. Instructions (A) and context (B) belong in project memory, and model choice (D) is configuration.

questions.stem: Claude Code performs well for one engineer and inconsistently across the team. What is the most likely cause?
options: The others need more capable machines
The repository is too large
The others are using different terminals
The working conventions live in one person's local setup rather than in the repository
questions.explanation: Context that is not committed does not travel, which produces exactly this asymmetry. Hardware (A), repository size (B), and terminal choice (C) do not explain a difference in output quality.

questions.stem: A pipeline requires output that always validates against a schema. What is the correct approach?
options: Declare the schema as a tool the model must call, and validate on receipt
Ask for the schema in the prompt and validate afterwards
Ask for JSON and repair malformed output in code
Use a lower temperature
questions.explanation: A declared schema makes the structure part of the contract rather than a request, and validation on receipt closes the loop. Prompt requests (B), downstream repair (C), and temperature (D) all leave the shape to chance.

questions.stem: Extraction is accurate for common cases and fails on rare formats. What is the most effective response?
options: Raise the temperature to encourage flexibility
Add examples covering the rare formats and define what to return when a field is absent
Switch to a larger model
Ask the model to try harder on unusual inputs
questions.explanation: Rare cases fail because they are unspecified, and examples plus an explicit absent-field rule specify them. Temperature (A) adds variance, a larger model (C) is not aimed at the gap, and exhortation (D) is not a specification.

questions.stem: What should a schema define for a field the source document may not contain?
options: Nothing, since the model will omit it
A default value that looks plausible
An explicit representation for absence, so a missing value is distinguishable from an unfilled one
A free-text field for notes
questions.explanation: Absence must be representable, or downstream code cannot tell a genuine gap from a failure. Silent omission (A) is ambiguous, plausible defaults (B) fabricate data, and a notes field (D) does not make the state machine-readable.

questions.stem: Which practice most improves consistency across a long-running structured extraction job?
options: Randomising the order of documents
Increasing the output token limit
Running each document twice
Fixing the prompt, the schema, and the model version, and recording them with the output
questions.explanation: Consistency requires that the things that shape output are pinned and recorded, so results remain comparable and reproducible. Ordering (A) is irrelevant, the token cap (B) affects length, and duplicate runs (C) measure variance without removing it.

questions.stem: A prompt mixes the instruction, the data, and the output format in continuous prose. What is the first improvement?
options: Separate the sections so the instruction, the input, and the required format are distinguishable
Shorten it
Move it into the system prompt
Add emphasis to the format requirement
questions.explanation: Structure lets the model tell instruction from data, which is the most common source of confusion in long prompts. Shortening (B) may remove needed detail, relocation (C) does not clarify, and emphasis (D) does not separate.

questions.stem: What is the strongest indicator that a tool surface needs redesign?
options: It contains more than ten tools
The model regularly selects a tool that cannot accomplish the request
The tools return JSON
The tools are implemented across several services
questions.explanation: Repeated wrong selection is evidence that the tools are not distinguishable from their descriptions, which is a design fault. Tool count (A), return format (C), and implementation topology (D) are not themselves problems.

questions.stem: How should a tool that performs an irreversible action be designed?
options: With a description warning the model to be careful
So that it requires more parameters
So that authorisation and confirmation are enforced outside the model
So that it is declared last
questions.explanation: Irreversibility is controlled by the surrounding system, because a prompt-level warning is a request rather than a guarantee. Extra parameters (B) and ordering (D) do not constrain authority.

questions.stem: A tool returns a large payload that consumes most of the context window. What is the right change?
options: Increase the context window
Summarise the payload with a second model call
Call the tool less often
Return only what the task needs, with a way to request more detail
questions.explanation: Tools should return task-relevant results rather than everything available, which keeps context for reasoning. A larger window (A) postpones the problem, a second call (B) adds cost and a failure point, and calling less often (C) does not change the payload.

questions.stem: What belongs in a tool's description?
options: What the tool does, when to use it, and what its parameters mean
The implementation language and framework
The service level agreement
The name of the team that owns it
questions.explanation: The description is the model's selection guide, so it must answer purpose, applicability, and parameters. Implementation detail (B), service levels (C), and ownership (D) are irrelevant to the choice.

questions.stem: A long agentic run degrades in quality as it proceeds. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model version changed mid-run
Context has accumulated until relevant material competes with stale material
The temperature was set too low
The tools became slower
questions.explanation: Progressive degradation over a long run is the signature of context accumulation and drift. Versions do not change mid-run (A), low temperature (C) reduces variety rather than quality, and tool latency (D) does not affect correctness.

questions.stem: What is the right way to carry state across a compaction boundary?
options: Rely on the model to remember what mattered
Increase the context window so compaction is never needed
Write the decisions and constraints that must persist into an explicit summary that is carried forward
Restart the task after compaction
questions.explanation: Persistence must be deliberate, because compaction is lossy by design. Relying on recall (A) is unreliable, a larger window (B) only delays the boundary, and restarting (D) discards the work.

questions.stem: Which measure most improves reliability for a workflow that must not silently produce wrong output?
options: A larger model
A longer prompt
More examples in the prompt
A validation step that can reject output and trigger a defined fallback
questions.explanation: Reliability against silent failure requires detection and a defined response, which is what validation with a fallback provides. Model size (A), prompt length (B), and examples (C) improve the average case without catching the bad one.

questions.stem: What should be measured to know whether a production agentic system is healthy?
options: Task success against a defined criterion, plus the rate and shape of failures
Total tokens consumed
Average response time
The number of tool calls per run
questions.explanation: Health is defined by whether the system accomplishes the task and how it fails when it does not. Tokens (B), latency (C), and call counts (D) are cost and behavior signals that say nothing about correctness.

questions.stem: The agent occasionally answers billing questions using an order it looked up three turns earlier for a different customer. What is the architectural fix?
options: Increase the context window
Scope each conversation's context to one customer and clear or isolate prior lookups when the subject changes
Remove the lookup_order tool
Instruct the model to be careful about customer identity
questions.explanation: Cross-customer contamination is a context-scoping defect, not a window-size problem

questions.stem: process_refund fails intermittently because the billing backend times out. What should the tool return so the agent can behave sensibly?
options: An empty string
A message asking the user to try later
A structured error with a category and a retryable flag, so the agent can retry or escalate deliberately
The exception stack trace
questions.explanation: Structured errors with categories and retryable flags are what let an agent recover deliberately

questions.stem: Which condition should route a ticket to escalate_to_human rather than continue autonomous resolution?
options: The customer writes in a language the agent supports
The order is more than thirty days old
The conversation exceeds five turns
The request falls outside documented policy, or the agent cannot make progress after a bounded number of attempts
questions.explanation: Policy gaps and lack of progress are the documented escalation triggers; turn counts and order age are not

questions.stem: The agent sometimes calls get_customer when it should call lookup_order. What is the most effective change?
options: Rewrite both tool descriptions so each states precisely when it applies and how it differs from the other
Reorder the tools in the configuration
Merge them into one tool with a mode flag
Increase the model's temperature
questions.explanation: Tool selection runs on descriptions, so differentiation is the fix for confusion between similar tools

questions.stem: Backend conventions should apply only when backend files are touched. Where do they belong?
options: In the root CLAUDE.md so they are always available
In a path-scoped rule under .claude/rules/ with frontmatter matching backend paths
In each engineer's user-level configuration
In the repository wiki
questions.explanation: Path-scoped rules load conditionally, which is exactly the stated requirement

questions.stem: When is plan mode the appropriate choice over direct execution?
options: For every change, since planning is always safer
Only when the model is unfamiliar with the language
When the change is large or risky enough that a human should review the approach before edits are made
When the context window is nearly full
questions.explanation: Plan mode is a human review gate for approach, warranted by risk rather than universally

questions.stem: A repeated multi-step review procedure should be available to the whole team as a single invocation. What is the right mechanism?
options: A shared document describing the steps
A longer CLAUDE.md
A saved chat transcript
A custom slash command or skill committed to the repository
questions.explanation: Repeatable team procedures belong in committed commands or skills, not prose

questions.stem: Subagents return full source documents to the coordinator, which then exceeds its context limit. What is the correct design change?
options: Have subagents return structured findings with citations while raw sources stay at the edge or in a scratchpad
Give the coordinator a larger model
Reduce the number of subagents to one
Truncate each document to its first page
questions.explanation: Delegation exists to keep bulk at the edge and move distilled results

questions.stem: Final reports attribute claims to the wrong sources even though each subagent is individually accurate. What is the likely cause?
options: The synthesis model is too small
The handoff format does not carry claim and source together, so provenance is lost between stages
The search subagent returns too many results
Reports are generated before analysis completes
questions.explanation: Provenance survives handoffs only when the format carries claim and source together

questions.stem: A subagent fails permanently on one source. What should the coordinator receive?
options: Nothing, so the report proceeds
A silent retry loop until it succeeds
A propagated error with enough context to decide between retry, exclusion with a noted gap, or abort
A generic failure flag with no detail
questions.explanation: Errors must propagate with enough context for the coordinator to choose a recovery path

questions.stem: The reviewer must emit results a pipeline can parse. Which invocation is correct?
options: Interactive session with output redirected to a log
Plan mode with an approval step
A cron job that emails the transcript
Non-interactive print mode with JSON output and a schema
questions.explanation: CI requires non-interactive invocation with structured, schema-validated output

questions.stem: Reviews flag many low-value style nits and engineers now ignore them. Which change addresses this?
options: Define explicit review criteria and a severity bar in the prompt, with examples of in-scope and out-of-scope findings
Post findings to a separate channel
Run the review only on large pull requests
Cap output at five findings
questions.explanation: Precision comes from explicit criteria and examples that draw the signal boundary

questions.stem: Some invoices legitimately lack a delivery date. How should the schema express this?
options: Make the field required and let extraction fail
Make the field nullable so absence is recorded explicitly, with conditional validation where the document type requires it
Omit the field from the schema
Default it to today's date
questions.explanation: Nullable fields record legitimate absence; required fields force fabrication or failure

questions.stem: Which loop gives the most reliable extraction output?
options: Generate, then manually review every record
Generate three times and take the majority
Enforce a JSON schema through tool use, validate, and on failure retry with the validation error provided to the model
Generate with temperature zero and accept the result
questions.explanation: Schema enforcement plus a validation-retry loop is the reliability pattern the guide describes

questions.stem: Your team reports 97% accuracy measured only on records that passed validation. Why is that number misleading?
options: Accuracy should be measured per field, not per record
97% is too low to report
Validation and accuracy are unrelated
It excludes the failures, so it measures where the system already succeeded rather than the true rate across all documents
questions.explanation: Measuring only validated records is a biased sample; calibration needs coverage of all documents

questions.stem: A pipeline has four steps whose order never varies and whose outputs are each checkable. What should it be?
options: An agent that plans each run
Four agents, one per step
A deterministic workflow with model calls at defined points
A single prompt covering all four steps
questions.explanation: A known fixed order is encoded rather than rediscovered, which is cheaper and testable per step. Runtime planning (A, B) adds nondeterminism, and one prompt (D) removes the checkpoints

questions.stem: What is the principal cost of introducing a subagent?
options: It loses the context the parent held unless the handoff carries it explicitly
It requires a larger model
It cannot use tools
It doubles token cost in every case
questions.explanation: Delegation buys isolation and pays in context, which is why handoffs must be explicit. A subagent does not require a larger model (B), can use tools (C), and cost varies with the work (D)

questions.stem: An autonomous step would modify production data. What does the architecture require?
options: A more capable model
A longer system prompt describing caution
A retry policy
A checkpoint where a person authorises the action, or a reversible mechanism
questions.explanation: Irreversible external effects need an authorisation boundary or reversibility, enforced outside the model. Capability (A), instruction (B), and retries (C) do not bound the consequence

questions.stem: What most helps diagnose an agentic failure after the fact?
options: The final output alone
A trace of each step's inputs, tool calls, and outputs
The total token count
The model version
questions.explanation: A per-step trace reconstructs a nondeterministic run, which is what diagnosis needs. The final output (A), token totals (C), and version (D) do not show where it diverged

questions.stem: Where should repository-wide conventions for Claude Code live?
options: In each developer's local configuration
In a CLAUDE.md committed to the repository
In the team's chat channel
In the CI configuration only
questions.explanation: Committed project memory is shared, versioned, and reviewed with the code. Local configuration (A) does not propagate, chat (C) is not read as context, and CI (D) covers automation rather than interactive work

questions.stem: Which task is best suited to headless Claude Code in CI?
options: Exploratory debugging of an unfamiliar failure
Designing a new module's architecture
Pair programming with a developer
A repeatable, well-specified check that runs on every pull request
questions.explanation: Headless execution suits bounded, repeatable work that runs unattended. Exploration (A), design (B), and pairing (C) all depend on a person in the loop

questions.stem: What is a hook for?
options: Running a deterministic action at a defined point, independently of the model
Storing reusable instructions
Holding project context
Selecting the model
questions.explanation: Hooks execute as code at fixed points, which is how a guarantee is enforced. Instructions (B) and context (C) belong in project memory, and model choice (D) is configuration

questions.stem: A pipeline needs output that always conforms to a fixed shape. What is the correct mechanism?
options: Requesting the shape in the prompt and parsing the result
Post-processing prose with regular expressions
Declaring the shape as a schema the model must satisfy, and validating on receipt
Lowering the temperature
questions.explanation: A declared schema makes the shape a contract rather than a request, and validation closes the loop. Prompt requests (A), text parsing (B), and temperature (D) leave the shape to chance
