questions.stem: How should a schema handle a value the source may not contain?
options: Omit the field silently
Supply a plausible default
Return an empty string in all cases
Define an explicit representation for absence
questions.explanation: Absence must be representable so a genuine gap is distinguishable from a failure. Silent omission (A) is ambiguous, a plausible default (B) fabricates, and an empty string (C) conflates absence with an empty value

questions.stem: Extraction succeeds on typical inputs and fails on unusual ones. What is the most effective response?
options: Raise the temperature
Use a larger model
Add examples covering the unusual formats and state what to return when a field is missing
Ask the model to be careful with unusual inputs
questions.explanation: The unusual cases fail because they were never specified, and examples plus a missing-value rule specify them. Temperature (A) adds variance, model size (B) is not aimed at the gap, and exhortation (D) is not specification

questions.stem: What is the clearest sign that a tool surface needs redesign rather than better prompting?
options: It exposes more than five tools
The model repeatedly selects a tool that cannot satisfy the request
The tools are implemented in different services
The tools return large payloads
questions.explanation: Repeated wrong selection indicates the tools are not distinguishable from their descriptions, which is a design fault. Tool count (A) and implementation topology (C) are not faults, and payload size (D) is a separate problem

questions.stem: How should a tool that deletes records be constrained?
options: By enforcing authorisation and scope outside the model
By a description warning the model to use it carefully
By requiring more parameters
By declaring it last among the tools
questions.explanation: Destructive capability is bounded by the surrounding system, since a description is a request rather than a control. Extra parameters (C) and ordering (D) do not limit authority

questions.stem: An MCP integration exposes an entire database through one general query tool. What is the architectural concern?
options: The model's authority is unbounded, and least privilege cannot be applied
It will be slow
It uses too many tokens
It cannot return structured output
questions.explanation: A single unrestricted tool removes the ability to scope what the model may reach. Speed (B) and tokens (C) are secondary, and structured output (D) is achievable either way

questions.stem: Quality degrades steadily through a long agentic run. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model version changed mid-run
Accumulated context has diluted the material that matters
The temperature is too low
The tools have become slower
questions.explanation: Progressive degradation over a long run is the signature of context accumulation. Versions do not change mid-run (A), low temperature (C) reduces variety rather than quality, and tool latency (D) does not affect correctness

questions.stem: What must happen for state to survive a compaction boundary?
options: Nothing, the model retains what matters
The context window must be enlarged
The decisions and constraints that must persist are written into an explicit carried-forward summary
The run must restart
questions.explanation: Compaction is lossy, so persistence must be deliberate. Relying on recall (A) is unreliable, a larger window (B) only moves the boundary, and restarting (D) discards the work

questions.stem: An agentic design calls the same expensive tool repeatedly with identical arguments. What does this indicate?
options: Healthy retry behavior
The tool is too fast
The agent is not retaining or reusing the result, which points at the state design
The model is too capable
questions.explanation: Repeating an identical call means the prior result is not available to the agent, which is a state problem. It is not retry behavior (A), and neither tool speed (B) nor capability (D) explains it

questions.stem: What determines whether two lines of work belong in separate subagents?
options: Whether each needs context the other would pollute
Their combined length
Whether they use different tools
Whether they can run in parallel
questions.explanation: Context isolation is the reason subagents exist. Length (B), tool difference (C), and parallelism (D) can all be handled within one context

questions.stem: Which design most reduces the cost of a wrong autonomous decision?
options: A larger model
A longer prompt
More tools
Making the action reversible, or gating it behind confirmation
questions.explanation: Reversibility and gating bound the consequence, which is what the risk is. Capability (A), prompt length (B), and tools (C) affect the chance of error rather than its cost

questions.stem: A CLAUDE.md has grown to several thousand lines. What is the likely effect?
options: Better results, because more context is available
The instructions that matter compete with material that no longer applies
No effect, since it is read once
Faster responses
questions.explanation: Project memory is context and dilutes like any other. More is not automatically better (A), it is not free (C), and it does not speed anything up (D)

questions.stem: What should be true of a skill before it is committed to a shared repository?
options: It is long enough to be useful
It encodes a procedure the team genuinely repeats, and it is reviewable
It is written by the most senior engineer
It covers every edge case
questions.explanation: A shared skill is justified by genuine repetition and must be reviewable like code. Length (A), authorship (C), and exhaustiveness (D) do not establish that

questions.stem: Why is committed configuration preferable to per-developer configuration for team conventions?
options: It is faster to load
It uses less context
It cannot be overridden
It is versioned, reviewed, and applies to everyone including automation
questions.explanation: Shared, reviewed, versioned context is what makes a convention hold across people and CI. Speed (A) and context size (B) are not the reason, and it can still be overridden locally (C)

questions.stem: A schema-validated response fails validation once in every few hundred calls. What is the correct handling?
options: Define a fallback path: retry, then fail explicitly rather than passing invalid data on
Ignore it, since the rate is low
Disable validation to avoid the failures
Increase the output token limit
questions.explanation: A rare failure still needs a defined path, and silently passing invalid data is the outcome to prevent. Ignoring it (B) and disabling validation (C) do exactly that, and the token limit (D) is not the cause

questions.stem: What is the advantage of validating structured output at the boundary rather than downstream?
options: It is cheaper
It removes the need for a schema
The failure is caught where it can still be retried or rejected, before it contaminates later steps
It improves model accuracy
questions.explanation: Catching at the boundary contains the fault. It is not primarily a cost question (A), the schema is what makes it possible (B), and it does not change the model's accuracy (D)

questions.stem: A structured extraction must record where in the source each value came from. What does this require?
options: A larger model
A longer prompt
A second extraction pass
The schema to include a provenance field the model must populate
questions.explanation: Anything the output must carry has to be part of the declared shape. Model size (A) and prompt length (B) do not create a field, and a second pass (C) is unnecessary if the schema asks for it

questions.stem: Two tools do nearly the same thing with different names. What is the architectural fault?
options: Duplication of code
Higher latency
The model has no reliable basis for choosing between them
Increased token cost
questions.explanation: Ambiguity at the point of selection is the fault, because the model chooses from descriptions. Code duplication (A), latency (B), and cost (D) are secondary consequences

questions.stem: What should a tool do when given arguments it cannot satisfy?
options: Return the closest result it can
Return a clear error stating what was wrong, so the model can correct the call
Return an empty result
Raise an exception that terminates the run
questions.explanation: An informative error keeps the model able to adapt. A closest-guess (A) and an empty result (C) are silently wrong, and terminating (D) discards a recoverable run

questions.stem: An MCP tool exposes a write operation that the use case never needs. What should happen?
options: Remove it, because unused authority is unnecessary risk
Leave it, since it may be useful later
Document that it should not be used
Rename it to discourage use
questions.explanation: Authority that is not needed should not be granted. Retaining it for possible future use (B), documenting (C), or renaming (D) all leave the capability reachable

questions.stem: What is the earliest reliable signal that context management has failed in a long run?
options: The agent begins repeating work or contradicting earlier decisions
The run takes longer than expected
Token cost rises
A tool returns an error
questions.explanation: Repetition and self-contradiction are the behavioral signature of lost state. Duration (B) and cost (C) rise for many reasons, and a tool error (D) is unrelated

questions.stem: Why is a defined success criterion necessary for a reliable agentic system?
options: It reduces token cost
Without it there is no way to tell completion from failure, so the system cannot stop correctly or be measured
It makes the prompt shorter
It is required by the platform
questions.explanation: Termination and measurement both depend on a definition of done. Cost (A), prompt length (C), and platform requirements (D) are not the reason

questions.stem: A reliability requirement says wrong output must never reach the user unnoticed. What does the design need?
options: A more capable model
More examples in the prompt
A detection step with a defined action when it fires
A longer context window
questions.explanation: Preventing silent error requires detection plus a response. Capability (A), examples (B), and context (D) improve the average case without catching the bad one
